title: How to Plan an Apliiq Capsule Around a Shared Set of Blanks
excerpt: A tight capsule built on two or three base garments looks like a brand and costs far less to sample. Plan blanks, palette, and decoration before you launch.
body: A capsule collection is the cheapest way to look like a real brand on a print on demand budget. Instead of dozens of unrelated products, you release a tight group built on the same few base garments, a consistent palette, and one decoration story that repeats across pieces. Because cut and sew suppliers price and sample by blank, restricting your blanks also reduces upfront cost and shortens the distance between a design idea and a live product page.

Choose the blanks before you choose the designs. Two or three base garments in consistent fabric weights will carry far more artwork than ten scattered products, and they let you photograph once and reuse the same assets everywhere. Pick blanks that are stocked reliably in your core sizes, then set a standing rule for the season: a new garment only enters the capsule if it shares a fabric weight or a colorway with something already approved. That rule sounds restrictive, and it is exactly what stops sampling cost from ballooning.

Limit the palette before you limit the artwork. Three neutrals plus two accent colors give every piece enough combinations to read as a collection while keeping each blank reorderable in sensible quantities. Product photography, size charts, and packaging all get cheaper when colors repeat, because a single shoot covers multiple listings. Shoppers also read a tight palette as intent, which does more for perceived quality than publishing another twenty unrelated products ever will.

Decide how decoration varies across the group. One artwork can run across several blanks, or one blank can carry a set of related placements, but doing both at once multiplies the files, samples, and proofs you have to review. Start the first drop with a single print method and treat embroidery or patches as a later capsule, once you know which blank and size mix actually sells. Sampling every combination in month one is the most reliable way a new apparel label burns its launch budget.

Plan availability before launch rather than after. Decide now what happens when a size sells through: whether you restock, keep the piece available as made to order, or retire it when the capsule window closes. Cut and sew production runs have real lead times, so this decision determines whether a surprise best seller becomes a restock or a stockout that sends buyers to a competitor. Publish the capsule window on the product page so expectations are set at the moment of purchase rather than in an apology email later.

Close the loop after the window ends. Compare which blanks, colors, and sizes actually sold, and promote the winners into your permanent catalog rather than keeping the whole capsule alive. That is how a seasonal experiment turns into a core line with predictable reorder volume. The DTCwise Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and the Apliiq listing at /tool/apliiq is where you can confirm which blanks, print methods, and minimums apply before you commit to the samples.
